chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Tiny Hill's illness, death and his Denver property
summary: Tiny phoned Horace weakened by illness in Denver, then died. He had owned a Fort Lupton farm, a radio station and a gas station and bought houses people lost.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: So here a few months ago, right here in Denver, Colorado, I was playing out, I think, a job -- I think it was out to a town near Villa, and Ike Cole was appearing here for a week. That's Nat's brother, of course. And Tiny heard that my band was playing with Ike there and backing him, and he must have gotten the time wrong because it was a week engagement, and he told me this on the phone -- he went out to hear me, and when he called me up, I almost cried because he had lost his voice, you know. He was real ill and He'd lost so many pounds. And he went to the union and got my telephone number, through the union here, you know, over the musicians' (unintelligible) local. And he called me up, and we talked, and he was telling me how ill he'd been and whatnot, and I felt so bad because I wanted to remember him as the days of when we had fun, you know.
And I talked to the guy like today, and a week later I was supposed to see him, and I read an article in the paper where Tiny Hill had passed. And that hurt me no end, you know.
So we lost a good one, because he was a great guy to arrangers and musicians and everybody, you

know, and he was helpful financially to guys. He had a big farm there, Fort Luyton, Colorado, and at one time he had a 24 hour radio station that he owned. And up until the time that he became ill and he had to move out again I think he sold all this. He moved right down the street here, oh, about eight blocks, at 32nd and Colorado Boulevard. He owned the property there.
He owned -- you know, when -- there was a project going there, and a lot of people bought homes -- they lost them. So Tiny bought up the difference on those things. He was a good businessman.
He told me this. And he used to own that gas station right over there.
Yeah, there's a Phillips, I think.
And I saw him there one day in his car. I said, 'What you doing here?' He said, 'I own this.'
Well, he was -- he was quite a guy.
